context: Definite articles: le (m), la (f), l' (before a vowel or silent h), les (plural).
Indefinite articles. 'Des' has no English equivalent: 'des amis' = (some) friends.
Gender must be learned with each noun: le soleil (m), la lune (f). Learn nouns with their article!

front: J'aime le chocolat, mais je mange une pomme.
pronunciation: [zhem luh shoh-koh-LAH, meh zhuh mahnzh ün PUM]
back: I like chocolate, but I'm eating an apple.
context: 'Le' for things in general (chocolate as a whole); 'un/une' for one specific item.

front: L'hôtel et l'école sont près d'ici.
back: The hotel and the school are near here.
context: Elision: le/la become l' before a vowel or a silent h.

front: je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles
pronunciation: [zhuh, tü, eel, el, ohn, noo, voo, eel, el]
back: I, you, he, she, one/we, we, you, they (m), they (f)
context: Subject pronouns. 'Ils' is used for any group that includes at least one man.
'On' = people in general, or 'we' in everyday speech. It always takes the il/elle verb form.

back: Shall we see each other tomorrow?
context: 'On' replaces 'nous' in conversation: on = we.
'Tu' for friends, family, children and peers; 'vous' for strangers, elders, at work, and for groups. When in doubt, use vous.

back: Can we use 'tu' with each other?
context: 'Tutoyer' = to use tu; 'vouvoyer' = to use vous. Usually the older or senior person proposes it.
Stressed pronouns (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles) add emphasis.
Stressed pronouns are used alone or after 'et', 'avec', 'pour': avec moi, pour lui.
After prepositions, use stressed pronouns: avec toi (never 'avec tu').

front: J'aime le café et le thé.
context: 'Et' = and. Never pronounce the t.

front: Tu veux du thé ou du café ?
pronunciation: [tü vuh dü TAY oo dü kah-FAY]
back: Do you want tea or coffee?
context: 'Ou' = or. Don't confuse it with 'où' = where.
'Mais' = but.

front: Je reste à la maison parce qu'il pleut.
pronunciation: [zhuh rest ah lah meh-ZOHN pars keel PLUH]
back: I'm staying home because it's raining.
context: 'Parce que' = because. 'Que' becomes 'qu'' before a vowel.

front: Il pleut, donc je prends mon parapluie.
pronunciation: [eel PLUH, dohnk zhuh prahn mohn pah-rah-PLWEE]
back: It's raining, so I'm taking my umbrella.
context: 'Donc' = so / therefore.

front: Je mange, puis je fais la vaisselle.
pronunciation: [zhuh MAHNZH, pwee zhuh feh lah veh-SEL]
back: I eat, then I do the dishes.
context: 'Puis' / 'ensuite' = then. 'D'abord… ensuite… enfin' = first… then… finally.
'Quand' = when. Linked before a vowel: [kahn tü].
'Aussi' = also, too. 'Moi aussi' = me too; 'moi non plus' = me neither.

front: Je parle un peu français, mais pas très bien.
pronunciation: [zhuh parl an puh frahn-SEH, meh pah treh BYAN]
back: I speak a little French, but not very well.
context: 'Très' = very; 'un peu' = a little; 'beaucoup' = a lot.

front: Les enfants jouent dans le jardin.
back: The children are playing in the garden.
context: 'Les' links before a vowel: [lay zahn-FAHN]. The -ent verb ending is silent.
'Elles' = they, for an all-female group.
'Pour' = for.

front: Il y a des pommes et une orange.
pronunciation: [eel yah day PUM ay ün oh-RAHNZH]
back: There are some apples and an orange.
context: 'Des' = plural of un/une.
After negation, un/une/des become 'de': j'ai une voiture → je n'ai pas DE voiture.

front: Le français, c'est difficile, mais c'est beau.
pronunciation: [luh frahn-SEH, seh dee-fee-SEEL, meh seh BOH]
back: French is difficult, but it's beautiful.
context: A typical French structure: topic first, then 'c'est'.
'Qui' = who. After 'c'est', use stressed pronouns: c'est moi, c'est lui, c'est elle.

front: Il ne parle ni anglais ni espagnol.
pronunciation: [eel nuh parl nee ahn-GLEH nee es-pah-NYOL]
back: He speaks neither English nor Spanish.
context: 'Ne… ni… ni' = neither… nor.
